STATUTORY CONVERSION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme LLC

CONVERSION DECLARATION
The name of the converting entity immediately before this conversion is Acme LLC, a California limited liability company. Pursuant to a statutory conversion under California law, Acme LLC has converted into Acme Corp, a California corporation, continuing as the same legal entity as Acme LLC without dissolution and without a separate transfer of Acme LLC's property, debts, or liabilities. The required approval for this conversion was obtained as follows: approved by unanimous written consent of the members.

GENERAL STATUTORY AUTHORIZATION FOR BUSINESS ENTITY CONVERSION
California law lets one type of business entity convert into a different type of business entity while continuing as the same legal entity, without a separate merger or dissolution and re-formation. This authorization is not contained in one single, entity-neutral statute. Instead, California has enacted parallel, entity-specific conversion statutes, each located within that entity type's own governing law: for a corporation, Chapter 11.5 of the General Corporation Law (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1150-1159) authorizes a corporation to convert into a different kind of entity, and authorizes a different kind of entity to convert into a corporation; for a limited liability company, Article 10 of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 17710.01-17710.19) does the same for LLCs, on both the outbound and inbound side. Each of these statutes independently authorizes the type of entity it governs to convert out to a different entity type, and to receive an inbound conversion from a different entity type, subject to two conditions that appear in both schemes: the law governing the entity type being converted into must itself permit formation by conversion, and the converting entity must comply with any other law applicable to converting into that particular kind of entity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A corporation may be converted into a domestic other business entity, foreign other business entity, or foreign corporation pursuant to this chapter"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1151(a), California General Corporation Law, Chapter 11.5 (Conversions), authorization for a corporation to convert into a different business entity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1151.)
  "A limited liability company may be converted into an other business entity or a foreign other business entity or a foreign limited liability company pursuant to this article"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.02(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, Article 10 (Merger and Conversion), authorization for an LLC to convert into a different business entity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17710.02.)
  Known gap: This corrects the framing this research started with. The general conversion authorization is not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 1150 alone (that section is only the chapter's definitions section) and it is not located in "Title 1, Division 3" of the Corporations Code. Verified directly, the corporation-side conversion chapter, Chapter 11.5 (§§ 1150-1159), sits in Title 1, Division 1 (the General Corporation Law), not Division 3. There is also no single chapter that governs conversions for every business entity type at once; a separate, self-contained chapter exists in each entity type's own governing law (this document verifies the corporation and LLC versions; a general partnership or limited partnership converting under California law would look to conversion provisions in its own separate governing statute -- the Uniform Partnership Act or the Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act -- which were not independently verified for this document). The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes (Cal. Corp. Code § 1151, in the General Corporation Law, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.02, in the LLC Act), not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that other states' conversion statutes (where they exist at all) work the same way. This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any entity and does not determine whether a specific conversion is available, permitted, or advisable for any specific entity.

CONTINUITY OF THE SAME ENTITY THROUGH CONVERSION
The core legal feature that distinguishes a statutory conversion from dissolving one entity and forming a new one is continuity: California's conversion statutes treat the converted entity as a continuation of the converting entity, not as a newly created entity receiving a transfer from the old one. Upon a conversion taking effect, all of the converting entity's rights and property -- real, personal, or mixed -- vest automatically in the converted entity; all of the converting entity's debts, liabilities, and obligations continue as debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converted entity; creditors' rights and liens on the converting entity's property remain preserved and enforceable against the converted entity to the same extent as if the conversion had never happened; and any lawsuit pending by or against the converting entity may simply continue against the converted entity, as if the conversion had not occurred. This means the property and debts do not need to be separately assigned, deeded, or assumed as part of the conversion -- the statute itself vests and continues them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "All the rights and property, whether real, personal, or mixed, of the converting entity or converting corporation are vested in the converted entity or converted corporation. (2) All debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converting entity or converting corporation continue as debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converted entity or converted corporation. (3) All rights of creditors and liens upon the property of the converting entity or converting corporation shall be preserved unimpaired and remain enforceable against the converted entity or converted corporation to the same extent as against the converting entity or converting corporation as if the conversion had not occurred. (4) Any action or proceeding pending by or against the converting entity or converting corporation may be continued against the converted entity or converted corporation as if the conversion had not occurred."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(b), General Corporation Law, effect of conversion: vesting of rights and property, continuation of debts and liabilities, preservation of creditors' rights, and continuation of pending actions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1158.)
  "All the rights and property, whether real, personal, or mixed, of the converting entity or converting limited liability company are vested in the converted entity or converted limited liability company. (2) All debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converting entity or converting limited liability company continue as debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converted entity or converted limited liability company. (3) All rights of creditors and liens upon the property of the converting entity or converting limited liability company shall be preserved unimpaired and remain enforceable against the converted entity or converted limited liability company to the same extent as against the converting entity or converting limited liability company as if the conversion had not occurred. (4) Any action or proceeding pending by or against the converting entity or converting limited liability company may be continued against the converted entity or converted limited liability company as if the conversion had not occurred."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, effect of conversion: vesting of rights and property, continuation of debts and liabilities, preservation of creditors' rights, and continuation of pending actions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17710.09.)
  Known gap: This continuity principle is stated in nearly identical terms in both of the entity-specific conversion statutes this document addresses: Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(b) (corporation as converting or converted party) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(b) (LLC as converting or converted party). The two citations below are to those two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's conversion under its own separate governing statute works identically (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). A closely related point -- that this continuity is also carved out of, and does not automatically extend to, certain provisions of California's own tax code -- is addressed separately in this document. This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any entity, vest any property, or determine the debts, liabilities, or pending litigation exposure of any specific entity.

APPROVAL REQUIREMENTS DEPEND ON THE CONVERTING ENTITY'S OWN GOVERNING LAW
The approval a conversion requires from the converting entity's owners is set by that entity's own conversion statute, and it differs by entity type. For a corporation converting out, the plan of conversion must be approved by the board and by the outstanding shares of each class; if the converting corporation is a close corporation, at least two-thirds of each class of outstanding shares must approve (though the articles may set a lower threshold, not below a bare majority). For an LLC converting out, the plan of conversion must be approved by all managers and a majority of the members of each class of membership interest (or, if the LLC has no managers, a majority of the members of each class), unless the operating agreement requires a greater approval -- except that if the conversion would make members personally liable for obligations of the converted entity, approval by all of the members is required, unless the plan of conversion instead gives every member dissenters' rights. When an entity of one type converts into an entity of a different type, the receiving entity's own statute separately confirms that the converting entity's approval is governed by the law under which the converting entity is organized, not by the receiving entity's own approval rules.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The plan of conversion shall be approved by the board of the converting corporation (Section 151), and the principal terms of the plan of the conversion shall be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of each class of the converting corporation. The approval of the outstanding shares may be given before or after approval by the board. Notwithstanding the foregoing, if a converting corporation is a close corporation, the conversion shall be approved by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of each class, or a greater vote if required in the articles, of outstanding shares (Section 152) of that converting corporation; provided, however, that the articles may provide for a lesser vote, but not less than a majority of the outstanding shares of each class."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1152(b), General Corporation Law, board and shareholder approval of a corporation's plan of conversion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1152.)
  "(1) The plan of conversion shall be approved by all managers and a majority of the members of each class of membership interest or if there are no managers, a majority of the members of each class of membership of the converting limited liability company, unless a greater approval is required by the operating agreement of the converting limited liability company. (2) However, if the members of the limited liability company would become personally liable for any obligations of the converted entity as a result of the conversion, the plan of conversion shall be approved by all of the members of the converting limited liability company, unless the plan of conversion provides that all members will have dissenters’ rights as provided in Article 11 (commencing with Section 17711.01)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, manager and member approval of an LLC's plan of conversion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17710.03.)

Corp. Code § 1201 for corporate reorganizations, or Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.12 for LLC mergers). Rather, each entity type's conversion chapter states its own, self-contained conversion-approval rule, which happens to track the general shape of that entity type's merger-approval rule (board-plus-shareholder-vote for a corporation; manager-plus-member-vote for an LLC) without formally incorporating it by reference. REQUIRED SECRETARY OF STATE FILING TO EFFECT A CONVERSION
A conversion is effected with the California Secretary of State through a single, combined filing, not two separate documents. When the converted entity is a corporation, the conversion becomes effective upon filing the converted corporation's own articles of incorporation, containing a "statement of conversion" that sets forth the name, form, and jurisdiction of organization of the converting entity and, if the converting entity has a Secretary of State file number, that file number (foreign converting entities must include additional statements about their own authorization and approval to convert). This same combined-filing structure runs the other direction as well: when a limited liability company converts into a domestic corporation, the LLC statute confirms that the statement of conversion is completed on -- and filed as part of -- the converted corporation's articles of incorporation, rather than as a separate certificate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The conversion by a domestic other business entity, foreign other business entity, or foreign corporation shall be effective under this chapter upon the filing with the Secretary of State of the articles of incorporation of the converted corporation, containing a statement of conversion that complies with subdivision (e). (e) A statement of conversion of an entity converting into a corporation pursuant to this chapter shall set forth all of the following: (1) The name, form, and jurisdiction of organization of the converting entity. (2) The Secretary of State’s file number, if any, of the converting entity."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1157(d)-(e), General Corporation Law, filing the converted corporation's articles of incorporation with a statement of conversion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1157.)
  "If the limited liability company is converting into a domestic corporation, a statement of conversion shall be completed on the articles of incorporation for the converted entity and shall be filed with the Secretary of State."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(3), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, statement of conversion completed on the converted corporation's articles of incorporation when an LLC converts into a domestic corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17710.06.)

There is a specific required filing, and it is combined with the converted entity's new organizational document as the assumption suggested -- but the required content is a "statement of conversion" embedded in that new document, not a separate certificate confirming the required approval was obtained (the statute requires stating that approval was obtained only for a foreign converting entity's statement of conversion, not for a domestic one). The two citations below verify the same combined-filing mechanic from both directions: Cal. Corp. Code § 1157(d)-(e) (from the receiving corporation's own conversion chapter) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(3) (from the converting LLC's own conversion article) are two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(1)-(2), which were not independently verified for this document). This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion. This document is informational only; it does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State and is not a substitute for the Secretary of State's current official forms and instructions.

EFFECT OF CONVERSION ON SHARES AND MEMBERSHIP INTERESTS
California's conversion statutes address what happens to the converting entity's outstanding ownership interests. An LLC's plan of conversion must state the manner of converting each member's membership interest into shares of, securities of, or other interests in the converted entity -- so the members' economic and governance interests in the old LLC become their interests in the new entity, on the terms the plan sets, rather than being cashed out or left unaddressed by operation of law. A corporation's conversion statute imposes an equal-treatment floor on the same process running the other direction: unless all shareholders of a class or series consent, each share of that same class or series must be treated equally with respect to any cash, rights, securities, or other property received in the conversion, and nonredeemable common shares of the converting corporation may be converted only into nonredeemable equity securities of the converted entity, unless all shareholders of that class consent otherwise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The manner of converting the membership interests of each of the members into shares of, securities of, or interests in, the converted entity."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03(a)(3), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, plan of conversion must state the manner of converting membership interests (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17710.03.)
  "each share of the same class or series of the converting corporation shall, unless all the shareholders of the class or series consent, be treated equally with respect to any cash, rights, securities, or other property to be received by, or any obligations or restrictions to be imposed on, the holder of that share, and (2) nonredeemable common shares of the converting corporation shall be converted only into nonredeemable equity securities of the converted entity unless all of the shareholders of the class consent"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1151(a)(1)-(2), General Corporation Law, equal treatment and nonredeemable-conversion protections for a converting corporation's outstanding shares (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1151.)
  Known gap: This confirms the framing this research started with -- membership interests and shares do convert into the equivalent ownership interests of the converted entity according to the conversion's terms -- while identifying the specific statutory basis for each direction: Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03(a)(3) requires the LLC's plan of conversion to state the manner of converting membership interests into interests in the converted entity, and Cal. Corp. Code § 1151(a)(1)-(2) imposes equal-treatment and nonredeemable-conversion protections on a corporation's outstanding shares when a corporation is the entity converting out. The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. Because this document's worked example is an LLC converting into a corporation, § 17710.03(a)(3) is the provision that governs that specific direction; § 1151(a) is cited to show the parallel, reciprocal protection that applies when a corporation is the converting entity rather than the converted one, not because it independently governs an LLC-to-corporation conversion. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's own governing statute imposes identical terms (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any interests and does not state the specific terms on which any specific entity's conversion will treat its owners' interests -- those terms are set by the plan of conversion the converting entity's owners approve.

TAX CONSEQUENCES ARE A SEPARATE CONSIDERATION OUTSIDE THE CONVERSION STATUTE
California's conversion statutes themselves flag that a conversion's continuity for state-law purposes does not automatically carry over into every area of tax law. Both the corporation and LLC conversion statutes state that a converted entity is treated as the same entity that existed before the conversion "for all purposes" -- except specifically for the purposes of the California Personal Income Tax Law, the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax provisions, and the Corporation Tax Law. The LLC statute adds that the conversion "shall not be deemed a transfer of property" for state-law purposes generally. Beyond what these two statutes themselves carve out, converting an entity from one type to another -- for example, an LLC taxed as a partnership converting into a corporation -- can carry significant, entity-type-specific and situation-specific federal and state tax consequences (including potential gain recognition), separate from anything California's conversion statute itself resolves. This document does not analyze federal tax law, the tax classification rules that apply to any specific entity, or how a specific conversion would be taxed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An entity that converts into another entity pursuant to this chapter is for all purposes other than for the purposes of Part 10 (commencing with Section 17001) of, Part 10.20 (commencing with Section 18401) of, and Part 11 (commencing with Section 23001) of, Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, the same entity that existed before the conversion."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(a), General Corporation Law, converted corporation treated as the same entity except for specified Revenue and Taxation Code purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1158.)
  "An entity that converts into another entity pursuant to this article is for all purposes other than for the purposes of Part 10 (commencing with Section 17001), Part 10.2 (commencing with Section 18401), and Part 11 (commencing with Section 23001) of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, the same entity that existed before the conversion and the conversion shall not be deemed a transfer of property."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, converted LLC treated as the same entity except for specified Revenue and Taxation Code purposes, and conversion not deemed a transfer of property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17710.09.)
  Known gap: This is a factual flag, not a tax analysis, and this document does not attempt to resolve it: the specific federal and state tax treatment of any particular conversion depends on the entities and elections involved (for example, an LLC's federal tax classification going into the conversion, and the mechanics of the specific transaction) and was not independently researched here. The two citations below verify only that California's own conversion statutes expressly except certain Revenue and Taxation Code purposes from the general continuity-of-entity rule -- they are not a statement of what tax result actually follows. Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(a) (the corporation conversion chapter) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(a) (the LLC conversion article) are two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources; note that the two statutes describe the same excepted Revenue and Taxation Code part with slightly different part numbers ("Part 10.20" in § 1158(a) versus "Part 10.2" in § 17710.09(a)), quoted here exactly as each statute states it, without attempting to resolve or reconcile that discrepancy. This document does not independently verify the substance of federal tax law (including the Internal Revenue Code's treatment of entity conversions and elections) or of the excepted Revenue and Taxation Code parts themselves. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California's own conversion statutes provide -- not a claim about which state's or country's tax law would apply to a specific entity's conversion, and not tax advice about any particular entity's own tax situation or filings.

AUTHORIZED SIGNER CERTIFICATION
The undersigned, Jordan Alex Lee, Managing Member of Acme LLC, certifies that they are authorized to execute this information sheet on behalf of Acme LLC in connection with its conversion into Acme Corp, and that the statements above regarding the conversion and its approval are true to the best of the undersigned's knowledge.

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Jordan Alex Lee, Managing Member

[This information sheet describes California's general statutory conversion procedure. It does not itself effect the conversion of Acme LLC or any other entity, is not the Secretary of State's official statement of conversion or the converted entity's articles of incorporation, articles of organization, or other organizational document, and does not constitute legal advice. The specific document required to be filed with the California Secretary of State, and the specific approval procedure that applies, depend on the converting entity's own entity type and governing law. The current official forms and instructions are published by the California Secretary of State.]

Notwithstanding the foregoing, if a converting corporation is a close corporation, the conversion shall be approved by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of each class, or a greater vote if required in the articles, of outstanding shares (Section 152) of that converting corporation; provided, however, that the articles may provide for a lesser vote, but not less than a majority of the outstanding shares of each class.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, manager and member approval of an LLC's plan of conversion
citations.quote: (1) The plan of conversion shall be approved by all managers and a majority of the members of each class of membership interest or if there are no managers, a majority of the members of each class of membership of the converting limited liability company, unless a greater approval is required by the operating agreement of the converting limited liability company. (2) However, if the members of the limited liability company would become personally liable for any obligations of the converted entity as a result of the conversion, the plan of conversion shall be approved by all of the members of the converting limited liability company, unless the plan of conversion provides that all members will have dissenters’ rights as provided in Article 11 (commencing with Section 17711.01).

There is no single, uniform vote threshold that applies to a conversion regardless of entity type, and the approval requirement is not a direct statutory cross-reference to that entity's separate merger-approval statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 1201 for corporate reorganizations, or Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.12 for LLC mergers). Rather, each entity type's conversion chapter states its own, self-contained conversion-approval rule, which happens to track the general shape of that entity type's merger-approval rule (board-plus-shareholder-vote for a corporation; manager-plus-member-vote for an LLC) without formally incorporating it by reference. The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes (Cal. Corp. Code § 1152, the corporation conversion chapter, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03, the LLC conversion article), not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's approval requirements under its own separate governing statute work identically (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). This document is informational only; it does not itself approve any conversion and does not determine what approval a specific entity's specific conversion requires -- that depends on the converting entity's specific entity type, its governing documents, and (for an LLC facing potential personal liability on conversion) the specific terms of the conversion.

expectedJSON.body: A conversion is effected with the California Secretary of State through a single, combined filing, not two separate documents. When the converted entity is a corporation, the conversion becomes effective upon filing the converted corporation's own articles of incorporation, containing a "statement of conversion" that sets forth the name, form, and jurisdiction of organization of the converting entity and, if the converting entity has a Secretary of State file number, that file number (foreign converting entities must include additional statements about their own authorization and approval to convert). This same combined-filing structure runs the other direction as well: when a limited liability company converts into a domestic corporation, the LLC statute confirms that the statement of conversion is completed on -- and filed as part of -- the converted corporation's articles of incorporation, rather than as a separate certificate.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, filing the converted corporation's articles of incorporation with a statement of conversion
citations.quote: The conversion by a domestic other business entity, foreign other business entity, or foreign corporation shall be effective under this chapter upon the filing with the Secretary of State of the articles of incorporation of the converted corporation, containing a statement of conversion that complies with subdivision (e). (e) A statement of conversion of an entity converting into a corporation pursuant to this chapter shall set forth all of the following: (1) The name, form, and jurisdiction of organization of the converting entity. (2) The Secretary of State’s file number, if any, of the converting entity.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, statement of conversion completed on the converted corporation's articles of incorporation when an LLC converts into a domestic corporation
citations.quote: If the limited liability company is converting into a domestic corporation, a statement of conversion shall be completed on the articles of incorporation for the converted entity and shall be filed with the Secretary of State.

expectedJSON.gap: This confirms, with a correction, the framing this research started with. There is a specific required filing, and it is combined with the converted entity's new organizational document as the assumption suggested -- but the required content is a "statement of conversion" embedded in that new document, not a separate certificate confirming the required approval was obtained (the statute requires stating that approval was obtained only for a foreign converting entity's statement of conversion, not for a domestic one). The two citations below verify the same combined-filing mechanic from both directions: Cal. Corp. Code § 1157(d)-(e) (from the receiving corporation's own conversion chapter) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(3) (from the converting LLC's own conversion article) are two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This document verifies only the specific case of an LLC converting into a domestic corporation; the required filing content differs for other entity-type combinations (for example, converting into a limited partnership or a domestic partnership, per Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(1)-(2), which were not independently verified for this document). This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion. This document is informational only; it does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State and is not a substitute for the Secretary of State's current official forms and instructions.

expectedJSON.body: California's conversion statutes address what happens to the converting entity's outstanding ownership interests. An LLC's plan of conversion must state the manner of converting each member's membership interest into shares of, securities of, or other interests in the converted entity -- so the members' economic and governance interests in the old LLC become their interests in the new entity, on the terms the plan sets, rather than being cashed out or left unaddressed by operation of law. A corporation's conversion statute imposes an equal-treatment floor on the same process running the other direction: unless all shareholders of a class or series consent, each share of that same class or series must be treated equally with respect to any cash, rights, securities, or other property received in the conversion, and nonredeemable common shares of the converting corporation may be converted only into nonredeemable equity securities of the converted entity, unless all shareholders of that class consent otherwise.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, plan of conversion must state the manner of converting membership interests
citations.quote: The manner of converting the membership interests of each of the members into shares of, securities of, or interests in, the converted entity.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, equal treatment and nonredeemable-conversion protections for a converting corporation's outstanding shares
citations.quote: each share of the same class or series of the converting corporation shall, unless all the shareholders of the class or series consent, be treated equally with respect to any cash, rights, securities, or other property to be received by, or any obligations or restrictions to be imposed on, the holder of that share, and (2) nonredeemable common shares of the converting corporation shall be converted only into nonredeemable equity securities of the converted entity unless all of the shareholders of the class consent

expectedJSON.gap: This confirms the framing this research started with -- membership interests and shares do convert into the equivalent ownership interests of the converted entity according to the conversion's terms -- while identifying the specific statutory basis for each direction: Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03(a)(3) requires the LLC's plan of conversion to state the manner of converting membership interests into interests in the converted entity, and Cal. Corp. Code § 1151(a)(1)-(2) imposes equal-treatment and nonredeemable-conversion protections on a corporation's outstanding shares when a corporation is the entity converting out. The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. Because this document's worked example is an LLC converting into a corporation, § 17710.03(a)(3) is the provision that governs that specific direction; § 1151(a) is cited to show the parallel, reciprocal protection that applies when a corporation is the converting entity rather than the converted one, not because it independently governs an LLC-to-corporation conversion. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's own governing statute imposes identical terms (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any interests and does not state the specific terms on which any specific entity's conversion will treat its owners' interests -- those terms are set by the plan of conversion the converting entity's owners approve.

expectedJSON.body: California's conversion statutes themselves flag that a conversion's continuity for state-law purposes does not automatically carry over into every area of tax law. Both the corporation and LLC conversion statutes state that a converted entity is treated as the same entity that existed before the conversion "for all purposes" -- except specifically for the purposes of the California Personal Income Tax Law, the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax provisions, and the Corporation Tax Law. The LLC statute adds that the conversion "shall not be deemed a transfer of property" for state-law purposes generally. Beyond what these two statutes themselves carve out, converting an entity from one type to another -- for example, an LLC taxed as a partnership converting into a corporation -- can carry significant, entity-type-specific and situation-specific federal and state tax consequences (including potential gain recognition), separate from anything California's conversion statute itself resolves. This document does not analyze federal tax law, the tax classification rules that apply to any specific entity, or how a specific conversion would be taxed.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, converted corporation treated as the same entity except for specified Revenue and Taxation Code purposes
citations.quote: An entity that converts into another entity pursuant to this chapter is for all purposes other than for the purposes of Part 10 (commencing with Section 17001) of, Part 10.20 (commencing with Section 18401) of, and Part 11 (commencing with Section 23001) of, Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, the same entity that existed before the conversion.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, converted LLC treated as the same entity except for specified Revenue and Taxation Code purposes, and conversion not deemed a transfer of property
citations.quote: An entity that converts into another entity pursuant to this article is for all purposes other than for the purposes of Part 10 (commencing with Section 17001), Part 10.2 (commencing with Section 18401), and Part 11 (commencing with Section 23001) of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, the same entity that existed before the conversion and the conversion shall not be deemed a transfer of property.

expectedJSON.gap: This is a factual flag, not a tax analysis, and this document does not attempt to resolve it: the specific federal and state tax treatment of any particular conversion depends on the entities and elections involved (for example, an LLC's federal tax classification going into the conversion, and the mechanics of the specific transaction) and was not independently researched here. The two citations below verify only that California's own conversion statutes expressly except certain Revenue and Taxation Code purposes from the general continuity-of-entity rule -- they are not a statement of what tax result actually follows. Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(a) (the corporation conversion chapter) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(a) (the LLC conversion article) are two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources; note that the two statutes describe the same excepted Revenue and Taxation Code part with slightly different part numbers ("Part 10.20" in § 1158(a) versus "Part 10.2" in § 17710.09(a)), quoted here exactly as each statute states it, without attempting to resolve or reconcile that discrepancy. This document does not independently verify the substance of federal tax law (including the Internal Revenue Code's treatment of entity conversions and elections) or of the excepted Revenue and Taxation Code parts themselves. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California's own conversion statutes provide -- not a claim about which state's or country's tax law would apply to a specific entity's conversion, and not tax advice about any particular entity's own tax situation or filings.
